title: Akbar and the Line Drawing (മലയാളം)
summary: Akbar challenges his courtiers to make a chalk line shorter without touching or erasing it. Birbal reveals a profound lesson in nobility. [ML]
full_text:
During a quiet afternoon in the Diwan-i-Khas, Emperor Akbar sat upon his golden throne in a philosophical mood. Courtiers and scholars surrounded him, each eager to demonstrate superior intellect. Akbar picked up a piece of white chalk from a table, walked to the center of the polished marble floor, and drew a straight white line about two paces long.

Turning to his assembly, Akbar declared: 'Here is my challenge to the wise men of Hindustan. You must make this chalk line shorter. However, you must not touch it, rub it out, erase any part of it, cover it with cloth, or scratch the floor in any way! He who succeeds shall receive a jagir of five fertile villages.'

The ministers hurried forward to inspect the line. One courtier suggested blowing air upon it, but the chalk remained fast. Another suggested pouring water near it, but Akbar forbade touching the floor. A third argued that if one looked at it from across the room, perspective made it seem smaller, but Akbar laughed and rejected the excuse. One by one, the nobles shook their heads and confessed defeat.

'Birbal,' Akbar challenged with a proud smile, 'can even your intellect shorten what cannot be touched?'

Birbal stepped forward with a serene bow. He took another piece of chalk from the Emperor's hand, knelt down beside Akbar's line, and drew a second line parallel to it—making his line twice as long and bold.

Standing up, Birbal gestured to both markings: 'Behold, Your Majesty. I have not touched your line, nor erased a speck of chalk. Yet compared to the new line I have drawn beside it, your line has instantly become shorter!'

The court fell silent for a heartbeat, then erupted into thunderous applause. Akbar smiled warmly and embraced his minister:

'Birbal, you have not merely solved a riddle; you have given us a timeless sermon. In life, petty men seek to diminish others by slander, jealousy, and tearing down their work. But the noble soul diminishes envy simply by expanding his own excellence and doing greater good!'
